facts.text: Etterbeek’s name likely comes from the Celtic word for “rapid movement” and the Dutch word for “stream,” first recorded in 1127.
In the Middle Ages, Etterbeek was a rural hamlet largely independent of Brussels, except for a beer tax granted to Brussels around 1300.
The town’s industrial roots ran deep, with chemical, clothing, metalwork, machinery, and furniture factories shaping its early economy.
Etterbeek is served by a single railway station, Merode, and three metro stops—Merode, Thieffry, and Pétillon—linking it to the capital’s core.
The neo‑Gothic Church of St. Anthony of Padua, built between 1905 and 1935, stands as a protected monument since 2004.
Paul Cauchie’s 1905 Art Nouveau townhouse, now known as the Cauchie House, remains a striking example of early twentieth‑century design in Etterbeek.
